newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Serb leader makes TV apology for secession call.
newsitem.headline: Serb leader makes TV apology for secession call.

text.p: Bosnia's Serb leader, reading from a statement she said was given to her by international election organisers, formally apologised on television on Friday for campaigning for union with Serbia.

In an extraordinary eve-of-poll appearance, Biljana Plavsic, ultra-nationalist acting president of the Serb republic entity in Bosnia, read out a statement written for her by the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).
It contained a promise that the Serb Democratic Party (SDS) would work for a Bosnia in which "Serbs, Croats and Moslems will be able to live together in peace and dignity".
But she spoke with little enthusiasm. Before beginning to read, Plavsic told viewers: "I have been given this statement by the OSCE to read out to you". She then put on her glasses and began to read.

"The Serb Democratic Party (SDS), including myself personally, sincerely apologises for statements made during the election campaign which bring into question the territorial integrity and sovereignty of Bosnia-Hercegovina."
"The SDS deeply regrets the statements which mentioned the Bosnian Serb Republic as an independent state."

The OSCE elections appeals board ordered Plavsic to make an extraordinary apology on SDS-run Bosnian Serb television after reviewing videotapes of party rallies in the 72 hours since the $50,000 penalty was imposed.
The board said speeches that SDS leaders delivered to a rally in the northern city of Banja Luka "crossed that line" dividing free political speech and rhetoric advocating lawless action.
No Serb Democratic Party official was permitted to make another statement before or after the apology.

The OSCE had warned if there was any delay in making the statement, or if it was changed or disowned, three of the first five candidates would be removed from the SDS party list for the elections to the national assembly of the Serb Republic and their candidacies for public office would be terminated.

Plavsic and other SDS members have campaigned stridently for "independence" although Saturday's elections are intended to help reunify Bosnia as mandated by the 1995 Dayton treaty that all three ethnic factions signed.
Some three million people were eligible to vote for a new multi-ethnic Bosnian presidency and parliament, assemblies in the Serb republic and Moslem-Croat Federation, and cantonal councils in each.
Aleksa Buha, the Bosnian Serbs' foreign minister, tops the SDS slate of candidates for the Serb republic assembly. Plavsic is the SDS candidate for president of the Serb republic.

"The SDS would like to clarify to all its followers and people of the Bosnian Serb Republic that the Serb Democratic Party has fully committed itself to the implementation of the Dayton accords," Plavsic said.
"The Serb Democratic Party intention has not been nor will be to unite all Serbs in the Balkans in one single state."
She said if SDS candidates were elected they would commit themselves to associate and work with the elected officials from the Moslem-Croat Federation.
Critics say the OSCE has avoided disqualifying candidates or the entire SDS party, as it is empowered to do, for fear of seeing the party sabotage voting.
